◆ DOES THIS RESONATE?

You might be living this pattern if...

  • You were told your blood pressure is "fine," yet you get lightheaded when you stand, your hands run cold, or your energy crashes after meals.
  • Your numbers jump at the doctor's office, or swing from day to day, and nobody has asked what that swing is telling you.
  • You were started on a pill (or 3) without anyone checking your salt response, your sleep, your insulin or your minerals.
  • You feel tired, foggy, crampy or puffy-ankled on medication, and were told that is just the price of control.
  • You want to know what is actually setting your number, so you can work with it instead of just suppressing it.
◆ The Assumption Worth Questioning

"If my blood pressure is normal, I'm fine. If it's high, I need a pill to bring it down."

In one study that followed 708 people for up to 27 years, salt-sensitive people tested after age 25 with normal pressure died at about the same rate as people with high pressure. Two people can share the same 128/78 and be living in very different bodies: one with flexible arteries and an intact lining, the other with a stiffening wall and a thinning lining. The number is the message, not the diagnosis. So what is your number trying to tell you?

◆ The Core Reframe

Your blood pressure is a message, not a number.

Every reading is the output of 3 levers (the pump, the pipes and the fluid) plus the conductor, your nervous system, which works all 3. High pressure, low pressure, and "normal but aging" are different settings on the same levers. Find your lever, and the plan writes itself.

The RoVive blood pressure model used throughout Parts 1 and 2. Pump: the heart plus its 3 helpers (the recoiling aorta, the breath and the calf muscles). Pipes: the lining (glycocalyx and endothelium), stiffness and tone of your vessels. Fluid: blood volume, salt, potassium, magnesium and water. Conductor: the autonomic nervous system, including sleep, stress, breath and the vagus nerve. A teaching model, not a diagnostic test.

What healthy actually looks like

Average is not normal, and normal is not optimal. The categories below are the US 2025 guideline categories for seated office readings. The RoVive target sits lower, as long as you feel well and stand without symptoms.

Category (office)Top / bottomWhat it means
Lowunder 90/60A problem only if you have symptoms or a drop when you stand
Normalunder 120 and under 80Risk keeps falling down to at least 115/75
Elevated120 to 129, and under 80The pipes and fluid are already talking
Stage 1130 to 139, or 80 to 89Lifestyle first for most; medication depends on overall risk
Stage 2140+ or 90+Usually lifestyle plus medication
Home runs lower above the normal range. Home and office agree up to about 130/80; above that, home runs lower: 135/85 at home is roughly 140/90 in the office. Judge yourself by a week of home readings, not one office number.
Common isn't normal. The Yanomami of the Amazon, eating almost no added salt, averaged about 96/61, with no rise as they aged. Rising pressure with age is common in modern life, not inevitable.
HOW TO READ THE CHART BELOW: "2x" means twice as often, compared with people whose usual pressure was 115/75. It compares groups of people over many years; it is not a prediction about you.
The risk of dying of a heart attack or stroke roughly doubles with every 20 points on the top number (or 10 on the bottom) above 115/75. Study population: individual data on 1 million adults with no vascular disease at the start, from 61 prospective studies, ages 40 to 69 for this doubling (more than 2x for stroke deaths, 2x for heart disease deaths); the relationship is about half as steep, but still present, at ages 80 to 89. Observational data. After Lewington et al., Lancet, 2002.
Optimal is 115/75 or lower. The study starts at 115/75 because that is where the data run out, not where the benefit stops: below it there were too few people to measure, and risk was still falling at that point. If you feel well and stand without symptoms, a usual pressure of 115/75 or lower is the target worth aiming for.

Lower is usually better, with exceptions

Nothing in biology is monotonic. Two large trials in older adults found that aiming lower cut heart events without more falls, in people who tolerated it. In SPRINT's group aged 75 and older (community-living, without diabetes, stroke or dementia), aiming for a top number under 120 cut heart events and led to 33% fewer deaths. In STEP (ages 60 to 80, China), aiming for 110 to 129 cut heart events by about a quarter, but did not reduce deaths, and low-pressure episodes were more common. A few situations call for caution:

Don't push lower when:
1. You are 80+ and frail, or you get dizzy or fall, especially on 2 or more pills
2. Your bottom number sinks under 70 with blocked heart arteries
3. You feel faint or woozy when you stand
4. It is the first days after a stroke
5. You have a tight aortic valve, or both neck arteries severely blocked
The heart muscle feeds itself between beats, during the bottom number. Study population: 22,672 people with stable coronary artery disease followed about 5 years (CLARIFY registry). Observational, so a low bottom number may partly be a marker of sicker, stiffer arteries. After Vidal-Petiot et al., Lancet, 2016.
A correction from Part 1: in Q&A we said stiff arteries need a higher pressure to feed the brain. The more precise version: if your arteries are stiff, don't chase a high top number. Protect your bottom number, and watch how you feel when you stand.

Measure it the right way

How you measure can move the number more than many supplements do. Every reading in this protocol assumes this method:

Before
  • Empty bladder
  • No caffeine, nicotine or exercise for 30 minutes
  • Sit quietly 5 minutes
Position
  • Back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed
  • Cuff on bare skin, arm at heart level
  • Right cuff size for your arm
Reading
  • No talking
  • 2 or 3 readings, 1 minute apart
  • Morning before coffee and evening, for 7 days

How strong is the evidence? The tier system

Discernment, not information volume. Every therapy, marker and mechanism in this protocol carries a tier badge, so you can see what is proven, what is promising, and what is still a question. Including a Tier 3 idea, and labeling it honestly, is part of the method.

Evidence tiers used throughout this protocol. Tier 1: consistent randomized evidence, and for markers, causal evidence. Tier 2: a real mechanism with smaller, mixed or surrogate-only trials, or large, repeated long-term cohort data. Tier 3: mechanism, a single association, or tradition only, or tested and found not to work for blood pressure.
How to use this protocol: start with the Decision Tree to find your branch and your lever, use the calculator in Labs & Targets with your own numbers, then build your plan from the Great 8 Pillars. Supplements and medications come after the foundations, not instead of them. The Slides tab holds both presentations.

Every protocol here was built from 20+ years of clinical pattern recognition, not what standard guidelines say. If you're ready to stop guessing, the full library is waiting.

◆ THE GREAT 8 PILLARS, RANKED FOR THIS PROTOCOL
Ranked by direct relevance to blood pressure. All 8 are important; the ranking shows where to focus first.
◆ HOW TO READ THIS LIST
All 8 pillars matter, always. The ranking reflects where the highest leverage points are for this specific protocol. Pillars ranked #4 to #8 are fully built out below; they simply have less direct impact on this condition than the top three. Your weakest pillar is often your biggest opportunity, regardless of its rank here. Numbers are points off the top number (systolic) unless stated.
#1
Movement
Movement trains all 4 pumps (heart, aorta, breath, calves), softens stiff pipes and quiets the conductor. In a 270-trial analysis of all exercise types, isometric training lowered the top number about 8 points, about what a standard pill does, and aerobic training lowered it about 8 points in people with high pressure. Mechanism: repeated bursts of flow raise shear stress on the vessel lining, which switches on nitric oxide production and remodels the wall.
◆ PROTOCOL-SPECIFIC ACTION
Start isometrics this week: 4 wall-squat holds of 2 minutes, 3 days a week, breathing throughout. Add Zone 2 walking most days and a 10-minute walk after your largest meal.

Why it is #1. Exercise works every lever at once: it trains the pump (heart, aorta, calves), softens the pipes (lower stiffness, better lining function) and resets the conductor (lower resting sympathetic tone). In the largest network analysis of exercise and blood pressure (270 trials, 15,827 people), every type of training lowered pressure, and isometric training lowered it most.

Typical drops in the top number. Isometric, combined, dynamic resistance: 270 randomized trials, 15,827 people, after Edwards et al., Br J Sports Med, 2023. Aerobic, if your pressure is high: 26 hypertensive study groups within 93 trials, after Cornelissen and Smart, J Am Heart Assoc, 2013. Resisted breathing (IMST): 36 adults aged 50 to 79, 6 weeks, after Craighead et al., J Am Heart Assoc, 2021. Slow breathing: 17 studies, after Chaddha et al., Complement Ther Med, 2019. Effects are averages; your response may be larger or smaller.

The isometric protocol Tier 1

  • Wall squat: back flat against a wall, knees bent to a depth you can hold for 2 minutes with effort (not pain). 4 holds of 2 minutes, 1 to 2 minutes rest between, 3 days a week.
  • Handgrip: squeeze a grip device at about 30% of your maximum for 2 minutes, 4 times, alternating hands, 3 days a week.
  • Breathe through it. Never hold your breath and bear down. If your resting pressure is 160/100 or higher, or you have heart disease, an aortic aneurysm, a recent eye or heart procedure, or diabetic eye disease, clear it with your clinician first; at 180/110 or higher, do not start until it is controlled.
  • Expect results in 4 to 8 weeks. Isometric wall squat ranked the single most effective exercise for the top number.

Aerobic: the aorta pump Tier 1

About 150 minutes a week of Zone 2 (e.g., brisk walk where you can hold a full conversation, easy cycling, light swimming, conversational-pace jog). In people with high pressure, endurance training lowered pressure about 8 over 5 points; in people with normal pressure, about 1 point. It also lowers arterial stiffness (pulse wave velocity) by about 0.6 to 1.0 m/s, more if you start stiff.

The calf pump Tier 2

Your calves are the "second heart": every step squeezes leg veins upward past one-way valves. Calf raises (2 sets of 15, twice a day), walking breaks of 2 to 5 minutes every 30 to 60 minutes of sitting, and a short walk after meals keep fluid out of your ankles and blunt the post-meal sugar spike that strips the vessel lining.

EECP Tier 2

Enhanced external counterpulsation: leg cuffs that squeeze in time with your heartbeat, usually 35 one-hour sessions. In a small sham-controlled trial, lining function (flow-mediated dilation) rose 51% vs 2% with sham. FDA-cleared for angina; for vessel health it is promising, not first-line. See Cutting-Edge Therapies.

Watch the exercise response: pressure is supposed to rise during exercise. A very large spike at moderate effort (for example, a top number above about 210 in men or 190 in women on a treadmill test) is a signal worth discussing with your clinician. Chest pain, unusual breathlessness or fainting during exertion: stop and get evaluated the same day.
#2
Food
The fluid lever lives on your plate: the sodium-to-potassium balance sets how much fluid your kidneys hold and how stiff your vessel lining gets. Salt raised around vessel cells (with aldosterone present, over 5 days) shrank their glycocalyx about 50% and stiffened it about 130% in the lab. Your 12-day salt test tells you how hard to pull this lever. A 25% potassium salt cut strokes 14% and deaths 12% in a 21,000-person trial.
◆ PROTOCOL-SPECIFIC ACTION
Use your salt-test result: salt-sensitive, cut sodium and switch to a 25% potassium salt (if your kidneys and medications allow); inverse, do not cut salt hard. Everyone: a potassium-rich plate and steady blood sugar.

The fluid lever lives on your plate. Modern diets run high in sodium and low in potassium and magnesium; ancestral diets ran the other way. That ratio, more than sodium alone, sets how much fluid your kidneys hold and how stiff your vessel lining gets.

Your salt, by your salt type Tier 1

  • Salt-sensitive (top number up 5+ on the salt test): this is your main fluid lever. Bring sodium down toward 1,500 to 2,300 mg a day and push potassium up.
  • Salt-resistant (within 5): salt is not your main lever. Moderate amounts, and spend your effort elsewhere.
  • Inverse (top number down 5+ when salt goes up): repeat the test to confirm. If it holds, cutting salt hard can backfire: when salt drops, renin, aldosterone and adrenaline rise. Roughly 1 in 7 to 1 in 9 people in the studies of the group that describes it.
  • Sweat a lot? Sauna, heat, long workouts or low pressure on standing: you need more sodium, not less.

Switch to a 25% potassium salt Tier 1

Outcome trials of potassium-enriched salt. SSaSS: 20,995 adults in rural China with prior stroke or age 60+ with high pressure, 5 years, 25% potassium chloride (Neal et al., N Engl J Med, 2021). DECIDE-Salt: elderly care facilities in China, 2 years. Taiwan: veterans home kitchens, about 49% potassium. Peru: 2,376 people, new high blood pressure. Most participants ate far more salt than typical Western diets, which may enlarge the benefit.

The tested mix: 75% sodium chloride, 25% potassium chloride. Make your own: 3 parts of your salt plus 1 part potassium chloride, by weight. A 25% to 30% potassium salt is the best-studied range.

Skip potassium salt, or use it only with a potassium blood test first, if you: have kidney disease or heart failure; take an ACE inhibitor, ARB, sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto), a potassium-sparing water pill (spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone, amiloride, triamterene), an aldosterone synthase inhibitor (baxdrostat), trimethoprim, regular NSAIDs, or potassium supplements; or have had a high potassium result before. Also skip it for children and in pregnancy (no trial data). In SSaSS, serious high-potassium events were no more common than with regular salt, but those at risk were excluded.

The plate Tier 1

  • DASH-style eating plus lower sodium lowered the top number about 11 points in people with high pressure, about as much as a drug. Lots of vegetables, fruit, beans, nuts, whole grains, fish, yogurt.
  • Potassium foods: potatoes and sweet potatoes, beans and lentils, leafy greens, avocado, squash, bananas, tomatoes, coconut water. Aim for about 3,500 to 4,700 mg a day from food if your kidneys are healthy.
  • Magnesium foods: pumpkin seeds, almonds, cashews, dark leafy greens, black beans, dark chocolate.
  • Nitrate greens and beets (arugula, spinach, beets): your mouth bacteria turn nitrate into nitric oxide. A week of antiseptic mouthwash raised pressure 2 to 3.5 points. Skip the antiseptic kind.
  • Food-as-medicine favorites (points off the top number, mostly in people whose pressure runs high): aged garlic about 9, hibiscus tea about 7, beets about 5, pomegranate about 5, cocoa about 4, ground flax (30 g a day) about 3. Kefir: great for the gut, no proven pressure effect.

Steady sugar protects the lining Tier 2

A sugar spike alone halved the glycocalyx (the vessel's protective gel coat) within hours in healthy young men, from about 1.7 to 0.8 L of glycocalyx volume. High insulin also tells the kidneys to hold sodium. Protein and fiber first, starch last, a walk after meals, and fewer liquid sugars keep the lining intact.

Weight, alcohol, caffeine and the hidden raisers

  • Weight: about 1 point lower on top for every kilogram lost Tier 1. Weight-loss injections (semaglutide) lowered pressure about 5 points, mostly through the weight loss.
  • Alcohol: cutting back helps in a dose-dependent way once you drink more than 2 drinks a day. In people drinking 6 or more a day, cutting back by about half lowered the top number about 5.5 points; at 2 a day or fewer, cutting back made little difference to pressure Tier 1.
  • Caffeine: raises pressure for a few hours in people not used to it. If your readings run high and jittery, run a 1-week caffeine-free experiment and measure.
  • Licorice (real, glycyrrhizin-containing), some energy drinks, decongestants and NSAID pain relievers (ibuprofen, naproxen) all raise pressure. Licorice can mimic an aldosterone excess: high pressure, low potassium.

Organ meats and Royal Lee's whole-food view Tier 3

Beef heart carries about 11 mg of CoQ10 per 100 g; beef kidney about 2.8 mg of riboflavin per 100 g. Royal Lee's Cardio-Plus carries 1.6 mg of riboflavin per 2-tablet serving, the exact dose that lowered pressure in people with the MTHFR 677TT genotype. There are no blood pressure trials of organ meats or glandular formulas. Go easy on organ meats if you have gout.

#3
Air
Breath is a pump and a conductor switch. Every inhale drops chest pressure and pulls blood home; every slow exhale tips you toward the vagus nerve. Sleep apnea, found in 64% of hard-to-control high pressure, drives night-time adrenaline surges and salt retention. And 5 minutes a day of resisted breathing dropped the top number about 9 points in 6 weeks.
◆ PROTOCOL-SPECIFIC ACTION
If you snore, wake unrefreshed or your morning readings run highest, get a sleep study. Add 5 minutes of slow breathing (6 a minute) daily; consider an inspiratory trainer.

Sleep apnea: the most common hidden cause Tier 1

In people whose pressure stayed high on 3 medicines, 64% had significant sleep apnea, by far the most common cause found. Every night, repeated drops in oxygen surge adrenaline and pressure, and the kidneys hold salt. CPAP lowered pressure most at night, and people who wore it 5 or more hours a night got about double the benefit. Clues: snoring, a thick neck, waking unrefreshed, morning headaches, night-time urination, high readings in the morning or no night dip.

Resisted breathing (IMST) Tier 2

30 breaths a day, 6 days a week, breathing in hard against a handheld resistance device at about 75% of your maximum (about 5 minutes). In adults 50 to 79, the top number fell from 135 to 126 in 6 weeks, about 9 points, and most of the drop was still there 6 weeks after stopping. The sham group did not change. Small trial, drug-sized effect, tiny time cost.

Slow breathing, about 6 breaths a minute Tier 2

In for 5 seconds, out for 5, for 5 to 15 minutes most days. Across 17 studies, slow breathing lowered the top number about 5.6 points. A long, slow exhale tips the conductor toward the vagus nerve.

Nasal breathing and air quality Tier 3

Nasal breathing keeps the airway more stable and adds nitric oxide from the sinuses; it has no direct pressure trials. Fine-particle air pollution raises pressure in population studies; a HEPA filter in the bedroom is a low-cost, low-risk move, especially near traffic or wildfire smoke.

#4
Sleep & Light
Pressure should fall 10% to 20% at night; when it doesn't, heart and kidney risk rise, and you cannot see it without a 24-hour monitor. Sleep is when the conductor resets, and light (morning daylight, sensible midday sun, darkness at night) sets the clock that drives the night dip and melatonin.

Your pressure should dip at night Tier 2

A healthy night-time pressure falls 10% to 20% below daytime. People whose pressure does not dip ("non-dippers") carry more heart and kidney risk, and a 24-hour monitor is the only way to know. Sleep apnea, late heavy meals, alcohol, salt sensitivity and stress are common reasons for a missing dip.

Morning or bedtime pills? Tier 1

Two large trials (TIME, 21,104 people; BedMed, 3,357 people) found no difference in heart attacks or strokes between morning and bedtime dosing. Take it when you will not forget. If your nights run high on a monitor, that is a conversation with your prescriber, not a default.

Melatonin Tier 2

Controlled-release melatonin at bedtime lowered night-time pressure (about 6 over 3.5 points) in small trials, without much daytime effect. Some beta blockers (propranolol, atenolol) cut night melatonin by 80% or more after single doses; in one trial, 2.5 mg of melatonin nightly helped people on beta blockers sleep about 36 minutes more.

Light on your skin Tier 3

Sunlight releases nitric oxide stored in the skin. In 24 healthy young people, UVA lowered the bottom number about 5 points for about 30 minutes, more than a heat-only sham. But 2 weeks of daily UVA in people with mild high pressure did not lower 24-hour pressure. Midday sun in sensible doses, balanced against skin protection. Red light therapy for pressure: very early, small and biased trials.

Sleep quantity Tier 3

Short sleep (under about 6 hours) tracks with higher pressure and new hypertension in population studies. Morning daylight, a consistent wake time and a dark, cool bedroom are the foundations.

#5
Spirit & Purpose
The conductor listens to meaning. Chronic threat, vigilance and unexpressed emotion keep sympathetic tone high; purpose, prayer, meditation and appreciation lower it. Transcendental Meditation lowered the top number about 4 points in pooled trials.

Whether that's God, your higher self, a deep belief in yourself, or simply what gets you out of bed before the alarm, this is your animating force. Purpose is not decoration: in pooled studies, people with a strong sense of purpose had lower rates of heart events and death.

Meditation Tier 2

Transcendental Meditation (20 minutes twice a day) has the most data: about 4 points off the top number across 12 studies, with larger effects in older adults and higher starting pressures. The American Heart Association says meditation "may be considered" as an add-on.

Heart coherence (HeartMath) Tier 3

Breathing at your resonance rate while holding a feeling of appreciation or care. One small workplace trial reported a 10-point systolic drop, but it was run by the company and has not been independently confirmed. Encouraging, not proven.

The pressure you carry Tier 3

Chronic vigilance, suppressed anger and unresolved grief keep the conductor in a sympathetic, high-tone state. See The Emotional Root in the RoVive Method tab.

#6
Water
Water is the medium of the fluid lever. Being even mildly dry thickens blood; drinking fast raises low pressure within minutes; regular sauna tracks with about half the risk of developing high pressure. EZ and structured water are fascinating questions with little human data, labeled honestly below.

Hydration is measurable Tier 2

Losing just 2% of body weight in sweat made blood about 6% thicker, and drinking water started to reverse it within 2 hours. Thicker blood is harder to push. Drink to pale-straw urine, more with heat, sauna or exercise, with electrolytes when you sweat a lot.

The water bolus for low pressure Tier 2

Drinking about 500 mL (2 cups) of water quickly raised the top number about 11 points in healthy older adults, and 33 to 37 points in people whose reflexes had failed. It works within minutes and lasts about an hour. A smart move before a long stand or a morning walk if you run low. Note: it also means a reading taken right after a big glass of water runs high.

Sauna Tier 2

Finnish men who used a traditional sauna 4 to 7 times a week were about 50% less likely to develop high pressure over about 25 years than those using it once a week. An association, not proof of cause. If you run low or stand up dizzy, rise slowly and rehydrate with salt afterward.

EZ water and "structured water" Tier 3

EZ ("easy") water is Gerald Pollack's exclusion zone: in the lab, water next to water-loving surfaces forms a band, up to several hundred microns wide, that pushes particles out. It reads negative, the water beyond it turns positive and acidic, and infrared light widened it about 3 times in 5 minutes and about 6 times in an hour. In chick embryos with the heart stopped, blood kept moving for about 50 minutes, and infrared took the flow from 41 to 153 microns a second. Other scientists see the same band and explain it with ordinary acid and salt gradients, with no new phase of water. No study has shown EZ water moves blood in a person or changes blood pressure.

"Structured water" is mostly a marketing term for treated drinking water, with no agreed definition and no agreed test. Liquid water loses the memory of its structure in about 50 femtoseconds, which is why physicists doubt any structure survives from a device to your glass. In Pollack's model, surfaces and light build EZ, not the cup.

Way to build EZ waterEvidence in people
Stay hydrated: water, electrolytes, water-rich foodTier 2 Blood measurably thinner
Infrared and saunaTier 2 Sauna association; EZ growth is lab-only
Sunlight on skinTier 3 Brief nitric oxide effect, not water
GroundingTier 3 10 people, red cells more charged; no pressure data
Plant gel water, chiaTier 3 Plant tissue builds EZ in a dish; never tested in people
Vortex, magnets, ice, "hexagonal"Tier 3 No published measurement in people; a UK regulator ruled "hexagonal" claims misleading
Analemma (wand or whole-house unit)Tier 3 Company-funded, unpublished studies; its main randomized trial had 13 people drinking it, measuring a blood energy marker (ATP), not pressure
Disclosure: Dr. Yoshi uses Analemma at home and has no financial tie to the company. It is a personal choice, not a proven therapy. It is also not a filter: it does not remove anything. If you want filtration, that is a separate device and a separate question (what is in your water), and that one has real data.
#7
Community & Connection
Loneliness predicted the top number rising faster year after year in adults over 50, independent of age, health conditions, medications and depression. Connection calms the conductor, and accountability is how plans become habits.

Loneliness raises pressure over time Tier 3

In adults 50 to 68, loneliness predicted the top number climbing faster year after year, independent of age, health conditions, medications, stress and depression: about 2.3 points more rise over 4 years per standard deviation of loneliness, and an estimated 14.4 points more for the loneliest compared with the least lonely (a model projection). Connection is a cardiovascular issue, not just an emotional one.

What counts: regular, reciprocal contact. A walking partner (2 levers at once), a weekly call, a group where you are known. This Circle is part of the plan: showing up, asking, and sharing your numbers is itself a lever.

#8
Electrical
The electrical pillar is mostly early for blood pressure. Acupuncture has the best data (about 6 points, fading after stopping); ear vagus stimulation is promising for the conductor; grounding and PEMF are tiny and mixed; hyperbaric oxygen raises pressure during sessions.

Acupuncture Tier 2

Real acupuncture beat sham by about 6 points on the top number over 22 sessions in a well-run trial, but the benefit faded within 3 months of stopping. Think of it as maintenance, not a cure.

Ear vagus nerve stimulation Tier 3

Transcutaneous stimulation at the tragus of the ear calms the conductor. In a small sham-controlled POTS trial, the standing pulse jump was 18 with the real device vs 32 with sham after 2 months. Blood pressure trials are small and early.

Grounding and PEMF Tier 3

Grounding: tiny, uncontrolled or company-funded studies. PEMF: 2 small studies hint at benefit in people with high pressure, with mixed overall results.

Hyperbaric oxygen raises pressure Tier 3

Hyperbaric oxygen has real uses, but pressure tends to rise during sessions. Get it controlled first.

EMF and screens Tier 3

No reliable blood pressure data. Bright screens late at night do delay melatonin and sleep, which matters through the Sleep & Light pillar.

Tier 1		Under 30 mg/gUnder 10 mg/gAn early sign of pressure damage to small vessels. Risk rises even within the "normal" range.
Fasting insulin
Tier 2		About 2 to 25 🤯Under 7, ideally 3 to 5High insulin tells the kidneys to hold sodium and stiffens the pipes. A range this wide is close to useless.
HbA1c
Tier 1		Under 5.7%Under 5.4%Sugar spikes strip the vessel lining within hours.
Uric acid
Tier 2		About 3.5 to 7.2 mg/dLUnder 5.5In 30 teens with new high pressure and high uric acid, 4 weeks of allopurinol lowered pressure (20 of 30 reached normal vs 1 on placebo). Fructose and alcohol raise it.
Aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Tier 1		Lab dependentScreen negativePrimary aldosteronism is a common, curable cause. Screen if pressure is resistant, potassium is low, or there is sleep apnea; the 2025 Endocrine Society guideline suggests screening everyone with high blood pressure.
TSH
Tier 2		About 0.4 to 4.5About 1 to 2.5, with free T4 and T3 in rangeBoth under- and overactive thyroid move pressure: low thyroid raises the bottom number.
hs-CRP
Tier 2		Under 3 mg/LUnder 1 mg/LInflammation predicts new high pressure and strips the lining. Calm it first.
ApoB
Tier 1		Often not orderedUnder 80 mg/dL (lower if plaque present)Pressure and lipids damage the same pipes together. See the cholesterol protocol.
Homocysteine
Tier 2		Under 15 µmol/LUnder 9In a 20,702-person trial in China, in a population without folic acid fortification, adding folic acid to a blood pressure pill cut first strokes 21%.
Ferritin
Tier 3		About 15 to 300 ng/mL50 to 150 (if POTS or low pressure)Low iron stores are common in POTS. Association only.
24-hour urine sodium and potassium
Tier 2		Rarely orderedSodium-to-potassium ratio under 1 (molar)The most honest picture of what you actually eat.
25-OH vitamin D
Tier 3		30 to 100 ng/mL60 to 80 (RoVive functional target, not a pressure target)Large trials show vitamin D does not lower blood pressure. Keep it in range for bone, immunity and mood; pair with K2.
Check the arithmetic: a home average of 115/75 gives a pulse pressure of 40, and 112/78 gives 34: both sit inside every target above. If your top number is 120 and the gap is 60, the bottom is 60: the gap is the warning, not the average.

Start broad (which pattern are you living?), then narrow to the lever. Most people carry 2 or 3 patterns. The calculator in Labs & Targets does this arithmetic for you.

The RoVive decision path. Home readings come first because one office number can mislead in either direction (white-coat and masked patterns). All thresholds match the Labs & Targets tab and the calculator.
Same day or emergency, before any lever work:
• Sudden weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, trouble speaking or seeing, confusion, the worst headache of your life, chest pain or fainting: call emergency services, whatever your blood pressure reads.
• 180/120 or higher with chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness or numbness, vision or speech changes, confusion or a sudden severe headache: call emergency services.
• 180/120 or higher without symptoms: rest 5 minutes, recheck, and contact your clinician the same day.
• Fainting during exertion, fainting while lying down, or palpitations that start and stop suddenly: get evaluated before training.
• Spells of pounding headache, sweating and very high pressure; or salt craving with darkening skin and weight loss: ask about adrenal causes.

Branch 1: High

Home average 130/80 or higher
High pressure: find the driver before you chase the number
High pressure is usually 2 or 3 drivers stacked: salt sensitivity, insulin resistance, sleep apnea, a hot conductor, stiff pipes, or a hidden cause like primary aldosteronism.
  • Run the 12-day salt test (skip the up phases if your home readings are 160/100 or higher, or you have heart failure, kidney disease or a prescribed salt limit).
  • Screen the hidden causes: sleep study if you snore or wake unrefreshed; aldosterone-to-renin ratio if resistant, low potassium or sleep apnea; thyroid; kidney function and urine albumin.
  • Check fasting insulin and HbA1c: insulin tells the kidneys to hold sodium.
  • Start the foundations together: isometrics plus Zone 2, potassium-rich plate, alcohol and caffeine audit, slow breathing.
  • If medication is needed, 2 low doses beat 1 high dose (see Medications).

Branch 2: Low

Top drops 20+ or bottom 10+ on standing, or symptoms
Low pressure has its own toolbox
Dizziness on standing, fatigue, fog or fainting. In older adults, check medications first: water pills, alpha blockers, nitrates, some antidepressants and too-aggressive blood pressure treatment are the common culprits.
  • Drink about 500 mL of water quickly before standing for long: the top number rose about 11 points in healthy older adults, 33 to 37 points when the reflex has failed.
  • Salt and fluids: for low pressure on standing, guidelines suggest 2 to 3 L of fluid and up to 10 g of salt a day, if your heart and kidneys allow it. Check a lying-down reading first: many older adults whose pressure drops on standing run high when lying down, and extra salt can push that higher.
  • Cross your legs and squeeze your thighs and buttocks when you feel it coming: fainting fell from 51% to 32% in people prone to fainting.
  • Waist-high compression stockings, or a belly binder (a wide elastic band worn snug around the belly when up).
  • Rise in stages; raise the head of the bed. Review every pill with your prescriber.
◆ A member's experience (Circle only)

A member shared that a pinch of salt in her morning water eased her dry mouth within days. One person's experience, but it fits the fluid lever.

Branch 3: The POTS pattern

Pulse up 30+ within 10 minutes of standing, pressure holds
POTS: when your pulse races as you stand
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome: a pulse jump of 30 or more beats a minute (40 or more ages 12 to 19) within 10 minutes of standing, without a pressure drop, with symptoms for 3 months or more. Mostly women aged 15 to 50. If you are over 50 and dizzy on standing, a pressure drop or a medication is more likely.
  • Why it happens: often 2 or more drivers: low blood volume (up to 70%), a deconditioned heart (about 13% smaller in 1 study), revved-up stress nerves, or small-fiber nerve damage that lets blood pool. Can follow a virus.
  • How it is found: lie down 5 to 10 minutes, then stand still. Pulse and pressure at 1, 3, 5, 8 and 10 minutes. Do it in the morning, with a chair right next to you and someone in the room. Then an ECG and labs (blood count, ferritin, thyroid, kidney function, electrolytes, morning cortisol).
  • Mainstream care: no drug is FDA-approved for POTS. Fluids, salt, waist-high compression, recumbent exercise; then low-dose propranolol, ivabradine, midodrine or pyridostigmine matched to the type.
  • The RoVive approach: find the driver first (blood volume clues, ferritin, mast cell signs, loose joints, a recent virus). Rebuild volume with electrolyte water and compression, with salt sized to your pressure. Retrain lying down first: rowing, recumbent bike or swimming for 3 months. Calm the conductor. Keep meals small and lower in carbohydrate.
  • Honest numbers: of people who finished 3 months of training, 71% no longer met the criteria, but only 41% finished, and many feel worse the first month. An ear vagus stimulator, 1 hour a day for 2 months, left the standing pulse jump at 18 vs 32 on a sham. A big sugar load raised the upright pulse 21%.

Branch 4: Normal, but aging

Under 130/80, but the gap is widening, there is no night dip, or it rises on standing
The quiet pattern: normal numbers, aging pipes
A normal average can hide stiffening pipes (a widening pulse pressure), salt sensitivity, or a missing night dip. Salt-sensitive people with normal pressure died at about the same rate as people with high pressure over up to 27 years.
  • Track your pulse pressure every few months; 50+ and rising is your early warning.
  • Pipes first: daily movement (stiffness down 0.6 to 1.0 m/s), magnesium (stiffness down 1.0 m/s at 350 mg a day for 24 weeks), K2, potassium-rich food.
  • Run the salt test anyway: it is the cheapest way to find a hidden sensitivity.
  • Consider a 24-hour monitor to check the night dip.

Then: find your lever

The 12-day salt test

The home salt test from Part 1. Down: under 1,500 mg sodium a day: home cooking, no packaged or restaurant food, nothing added at the table. Up: your usual food plus 6 g of salt a day (1 level teaspoon of fine table salt), spread over meals. Phase 3: the same 6 g of your own sea or mineral salt; weigh coarse salts. A teaching protocol, not a validated clinical test.
Who skips: the whole test if you take lithium (changing your salt intake changes your lithium level). The up phases if home readings are 160/100 or higher, heart failure, kidney disease, ankle swelling, or a prescribed salt limit; stop if you pass 160/100. The down phase if you have low pressure, get dizzy on standing, have POTS, or take a water pill.

Four patterns from the series

Composites with details changed. Each shows how the levers stack. To see the original case slides, open the Slides tab: Part 1, slides 14 to 16 (The Live Wire, The Smolder, The Wrong Room) and Part 2, slide 18 (The Three-Pill Puzzle).

Pump and conductor
The Live Wire
Woman in her 50s who feels everything: lights brighter, sounds louder. 170s over 110s after 3 cups of coffee.
  • Her pressure is a nervous system message, not a cardiology problem.
  • First experiment: take the caffeine out, then measure for a week.
  • Brakes: vagal device at night, sauna most days, puzzles while walking, yoga.
Pipes, with a fluid twist
The Smolder
About 190/110 caught by accident; fasting insulin 19, A1c 6.5%, visceral fat at the 87th percentile, ApoB 137, 30 sedentary years.
  • Insulin tells the kidneys to hold sodium; the pipes stiffen; nights may be the hidden driver.
  • The scariest reading is the one nobody takes.
  • Next: sleep study and calcium score.
Fluid, with pump and pipes
The Wrong Room
Early 80s, walks the hills with her dog every morning. Swollen ankles, dizzy when she stands: wet legs, dry pipes.
  • A stiff heart backs pressure into the veins; a thin lining and low protein let water leak; a weak calf pump lets it pool.
  • Diuretic swings and extra thyroid dry the pipes.
  • Pearl: potassium won't stay up without magnesium.
All 3 levers
The Three-Pill Puzzle
Water pill, amlodipine 10 mg, a weight-loss injection, and electrolyte packets 3 times a day.
  • Water pill: sodium fell to 128 (normal 135 to 145), tired and foggy. Fluid lever pulled too far.
  • Amlodipine 10 mg: ankles swelled; back to 5 mg, they eased. Pipes opened, fluid leaked to the ankles.
  • Weight-loss injection: sugar dips, night chills, racing pulse, a 161/84 surge. The conductor sounded the alarm.
  • Electrolyte packets: 3 a day meant more sodium and more swelling; cut to 1.

Read this first. This tab helps you have a better conversation with your prescriber; it is not a plan to change your medication on your own. Never stop a blood pressure medicine suddenly: stopping beta blockers or clonidine abruptly can cause a dangerous rebound in pressure and heart rate.

Every pill pulls a lever

Each major class lowers the top number about 7 to 9 points on its own. Knowing which lever a pill pulls tells you what to watch, and what to replace.

Class (e.g., examples)LeverTop numberYou may feelCan drain or raiseNatural ally
Thiazide water pill (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone)Fluidabout 7Low sodium; higher sugar and uric acidDrains potassium, magnesium, zincLess salt, more potassium
Loop water pill (e.g., furosemide, torsemide)Fluidmainly for swellingCramps, low potassiumDrains thiamine (B1), magnesiumB1 and magnesium-rich food; gentle herbal diuretics only with your prescriber
ACE inhibitor (e.g., lisinopril, enalapril)Pipesabout 7Dry cough in about 11%Drains zinc; raises potassiumHibiscus (milder than the drug)
ARB (e.g., losartan, valsartan)PipessimilarUsually littleRaises potassiumHibiscus, aged garlic
Calcium channel blocker (e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine)Pipesabout 8Ankle swelling in about 11%None knownMagnesium
Beta blocker (e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol)Pumpabout 9Tired, cold hands, poorer sleepLowers night melatonin (some types)Slow breathing, meditation
Potassium-sparing water pill (e.g., spironolactone, eplerenone)Fluidabout 9 more when 3 drugs fail (spironolactone)Breast tenderness in some men (spironolactone)Raises potassiumSkip potassium salt

Typical placebo-subtracted drops from standard-dose single drugs, after Law et al., BMJ, 2003 and 2009, and Wald et al., Am J Med, 2009. Cough rate from 125 studies (Bangalore et al., Am J Med, 2010); ankle swelling from 106 studies (Makani et al., J Hypertens, 2011).

4 principles that matter more than the brand

1 · It's the drop, not the pill Tier 1

Across 464,000 people, 10 points lower on top meant about 22% fewer coronary events and 41% fewer strokes, with classes similar within a few percent. Calcium channel blockers did slightly better for stroke; beta blockers had extra benefit in the first years after a heart attack.

2 · 2 low doses beat 1 high dose Tier 1

Across 42 trials with nearly 11,000 people, adding a second kind of medicine gave about 5 times the extra lowering of doubling the first. In QUARTET, quarter doses of 4 drugs in 1 pill controlled 76% vs 58% on a standard single drug at 12 weeks, without more side-effect withdrawals.

3 · Timing: whenever you won't forget Tier 1

TIME (21,104 people) and BedMed (3,357 people) found no difference in heart attacks or strokes between morning and bedtime dosing.

4 · Stepping down can be safe Tier 1

In people 80+ on several pills (OPTIMISE), removing 1 kept 86% under 150 at 12 weeks, close to the 88% who changed nothing; the top number ran about 3 points higher. Done with your prescriber, not alone.

Replace what it drains: potassium and magnesium with thiazide water pills; thiamine (B1) and magnesium with long-term loop water pills (in one heart failure study on higher-dose furosemide, 21 of 23 were low in B1). Melatonin is worth discussing on propranolol or atenolol.

Class by class

Thiazide and thiazide-like diureticsTier 1
e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide
LEVER: FLUID

What it does: Make the kidneys release sodium and water, then gently relax the vessel wall.

The honest case for: Cheap, long track record, strong outcome data, especially chlorthalidone and indapamide. Excellent partner for salt-sensitive people and for a second drug.
The honest case against: Drains potassium, magnesium and zinc; can raise blood sugar and uric acid (gout); low sodium in some older adults. Watch for fatigue and fog.
NUTRACEUTICAL ALTERNATIVE
Lower sodium plus a potassium-rich plate or 25% potassium salt (if kidneys allow and you are not on potassium-holding drugs), plus magnesium. Real, but smaller than the drug, and they also replace what the drug drains.
Loop diureticsTier 1
e.g., furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide
LEVER: FLUID

What it does: Powerful, short-acting water removal, mainly for swelling and heart failure rather than pressure.

The honest case for: Essential when fluid is truly overloaded (heart failure, kidney disease).
The honest case against: Cramps, low potassium and magnesium, thiamine depletion, dizziness on standing. Swings in volume can leave the pipes dry.
NUTRACEUTICAL ALTERNATIVE
No natural agent matches a loop diuretic for true fluid overload (heart failure, kidney disease). Support it with thiamine-rich foods (or a B1 supplement), magnesium, and calf-pump work for leg swelling.

Gentle herbal diuretics, for mild puffiness only and only with your prescriber (stacked on a water pill they can push sodium and potassium further out of range):
• Horsetail (Equisetum arvense)Tier 2: in 36 healthy men, a standardized extract (900 mg a day for 4 days) increased urine output about as much as hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, without changing electrolytes. Short-term, healthy volunteers, thiazide-strength at most. Choose a product labeled thiaminase-free: raw horsetail breaks down B1, the very vitamin loop diuretics drain. Avoid in pregnancy.
• Dandelion leafTier 3: in 17 volunteers, urination increased after the first doses on a single day; no control group, no pressure data. Naturally rich in potassium, so caution with potassium-holding drugs.
• Celery seedTier 3: yes, traditionally used as a diuretic, but that effect rests mostly on animal data; its small human trials measured blood pressure, not urine output. Avoid in pregnancy; can cause sun sensitivity.
• Hibiscus and parsleyTier 3: mild traditional diuretics; hibiscus also lowers pressure (see Nutraceuticals).
ACE inhibitors and ARBsTier 1
e.g., lisinopril, enalapril (ACE inhibitors); losartan, valsartan (ARBs)
LEVER: PIPES

What it does: Block the angiotensin system that tightens vessels and holds salt; protect kidneys, especially with diabetes or protein in the urine.

The honest case for: Strong outcome data; first choice for kidney protection; ARBs rarely cause cough.
The honest case against: ACE inhibitor dry cough in about 1 in 9; raise potassium (no potassium salt without monitoring); rare swelling of the lips and tongue (angioedema) needs emergency care. Not for use in pregnancy or when trying to conceive (risk to the baby); the same applies to spironolactone and the newer aldosterone blockers.
NUTRACEUTICAL ALTERNATIVE
A standardized hibiscus extract was tested head to head against lisinopril 10 mg: it lowered pressure, but less than the drug. Hibiscus tea (3 cups a day) beat placebo by about 6 points in a separate trial. Aged garlic extract works on a similar endpoint. Neither matches the kidney protection data.
Calcium channel blockersTier 1
e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine
LEVER: PIPES

What it does: Relax the muscle of the artery wall.

The honest case for: Strong outcome data, slightly better for stroke prevention; effective in older adults and people of African ancestry.
The honest case against: Ankle swelling in about 1 in 10, more at higher doses (16% vs 6% at low dose). The pipes open, fluid leaks to the ankles; it is not fluid overload, so a water pill is the wrong fix.
NUTRACEUTICAL ALTERNATIVE
Magnesium is nature's calcium antagonist, with a much smaller effect (about 2 points). Dose reduction, or pairing a low dose with a second class, often solves the swelling.
Beta blockersTier 1
e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol, atenolol
LEVER: PUMP

What it does: Slow the heart and soften each beat; quiet the sympathetic conductor.

The honest case for: Essential after a heart attack, in heart failure and for some rhythm problems. Low-dose propranolol helps some people with POTS.
The honest case against: Weaker for stroke prevention as a first drug in uncomplicated high pressure; fatigue, cold hands, exercise limits, poorer sleep (some types cut night melatonin by 80% or more). Never stop suddenly.
NUTRACEUTICAL ALTERNATIVE
For the conductor: slow breathing, resisted breathing, meditation and sleep apnea treatment. No supplement matches a beta blocker after a heart attack.
Potassium-sparing diureticsTier 1
e.g., spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene
LEVER: FLUID

What it does: Spironolactone and eplerenone block aldosterone, the hormone that holds sodium and water; amiloride and triamterene block the kidney sodium channel that aldosterone switches on. All of them hold on to potassium.

The honest case for: When 3 drugs fail, spironolactone lowered home pressure about 9 points more than placebo, beating the other options tested (PATHWAY-2). The targeted medicine for primary aldosteronism (one-sided disease can often be cured with surgery).
The honest case against: Raise potassium (no potassium salt); spironolactone can cause breast tenderness or enlargement in some men (eplerenone rarely does); needs kidney and potassium checks.
NUTRACEUTICAL ALTERNATIVE
Find out why aldosterone is high (screen for primary aldosteronism, check for licorice and sleep apnea). Sodium reduction amplifies the drug. No natural equivalent at comparable effect.
Weight-loss injections (GLP-1 class)Tier 2
e.g., semaglutide, tirzepatide
LEVER: ALL 3

What it does: Reduce appetite and weight; pressure follows.

The honest case for: Semaglutide lowered the top number about 5 points, mostly through weight loss, and reduced the need for blood pressure pills.
The honest case against: Can unmask over-treatment as weight falls (dizziness, low pressure); sugar dips and a racing pulse in some; muscle loss without resistance training.
NUTRACEUTICAL ALTERNATIVE
Berberine with meals (it interacts with many medicines, including cyclosporine and diabetes drugs, and is not for pregnancy or breastfeeding), chromium, 30 to 40 g of protein per meal and pre-meal viscous fiber support the same metabolic direction, with far smaller weight loss. As weight falls, ask your prescriber to review every blood pressure pill.

Medicines and substances that raise pressure

  • NSAID pain relievers (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen)
  • Decongestants (e.g., pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine)
  • Stimulants (e.g., ADHD medicines, some weight-loss drugs), energy drinks
  • Real licorice and some herbal teas containing glycyrrhizin
  • Oral contraceptives and some hormone therapies
  • Steroids (e.g., prednisone)
  • Some antidepressants (e.g., venlafaxine), cyclosporine, some migraine drugs
  • Alcohol above about 2 drinks a day; nicotine

POTS medicines, briefly

No drug is FDA-approved for POTS. Low-dose propranolol (20 mg) beat placebo acutely, and 80 mg lowered the pulse more but helped symptoms less. Ivabradine lowered the pulse in a small positive trial; in a 2026 trial of 181 adults with long COVID POTS it lowered the pulse but did not improve symptoms vs placebo (not yet peer reviewed). Midodrine helps the nerve-damage type more than the adrenaline type. Pyridostigmine helps some. The only IVIG trial was negative vs albumin. A lower pulse is not the goal by itself.

Foundations first. If you are pregnant, breastfeeding or trying to conceive, use none of the supplements or botanicals here without your clinician. Supplements add a few points; isometrics, potassium, sleep apnea treatment and weight move far more. Use these to fill gaps and fine-tune, not as a substitute for the levers. Check interactions if you take blood pressure medicines or blood thinners: many of these are additive.

EDUCATIONAL ONLY · NOT MEDICAL ADVICE · NOT A PRESCRIPTION · REVIEW ANY CHANGE WITH YOUR OWN CLINICIAN, ESPECIALLY IF YOU TAKE BLOOD PRESSURE MEDICATION

Typical placebo-subtracted drops in the top number from meta-analyses and trials, mostly in people whose pressure runs high; your response may be larger or smaller. Garlic shows the overall and high-pressure values. Vitamin C shows the high-pressure value. Riboflavin applies only to MTHFR 677TT carriers. Main sources: Aburto et al., BMJ, 2013 and Filippini et al., Int J Cardiol, 2017 (potassium); Ried et al., Cochrane, 2017 (cocoa); Zhang et al., Hypertension, 2016 (magnesium); Ried et al., J Nutr, 2016 (garlic); Juraschek et al., Am J Clin Nutr, 2012 (vitamin C); Wilson et al., Hypertension, 2013 (riboflavin).

Nutraceuticals

Potassium (food first, then 25% potassium salt)Tier 1
Mild: 3,500 mg/day from foodModerate: 4,700 mg/day from food + 25% potassium saltHeavy: Supplements only with your clinician and labs

Typical drop: about 3.5 points overall, 4.5 in people with high pressure; 25% potassium salt cut strokes 14% in SSaSS.

Form: food and potassium chloride salt carry the outcome data. US over-the-counter pills hold 99 mg or less each, because FDA rules require prescription labeling and a small-bowel injury warning at 100 mg or more per tablet. Potassium citrate or bicarbonate forms are alkalinizing, useful if you also form kidney stones.

Caution: kidney disease, heart failure, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, sacubitril/valsartan, spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone, amiloride, triamterene, baxdrostat, trimethoprim or regular NSAIDs: check potassium and kidney function first. Keep serum potassium 4.0 to 5.0.

Magnesium (glycinate, taurate or citrate)Tier 1
Mild: 150 to 200 mg elementalModerate: 300 to 400 mg elementalHeavy: 500 to 600 mg elemental, split

Typical drop: about 2 points (34 trials, median 368 mg/day for 3 months); more if you are low. 350 mg a day for 24 weeks reduced arterial stiffness 1.0 m/s.

Form: glycinate is calming and gentle; taurate pairs with taurine; citrate is more laxative. Evening dosing helps sleep.

Caution: loose stools mean the dose is too high, reduce by 100 mg. Avoid supplements with significant kidney disease. Serum magnesium is a poor marker; use RBC magnesium.

Omega-3 (EPA + DHA)Tier 1
Mild: 1 g/dayModerate: 2 g/dayHeavy: 3 g/day

Typical drop: about 2.6 points; 2 to 3 g a day of combined EPA and DHA looked optimal in dose-response analyses.

Form: triglyceride-form fish or algal oil with meals containing fat. Check your Omega-3 Index (target 8% or higher).

Caution: in heart outcome trials, omega-3 supplements raised the risk of atrial fibrillation: about 12% higher at 1 g a day or less and about 49% higher above 1 g a day. Talk with your clinician before taking 2 to 3 g a day if you are over 65, have heart disease or palpitations, or take blood thinners (added bleeding risk).

Cocoa flavanolsTier 2
Mild: 200 mg flavanolsModerate: 500 mg flavanolsHeavy: 700 to 900 mg flavanols

Typical drop: about 1.8 overall, about 4 in people with high pressure; improves lining function (flow-mediated dilation).

Form: a standardized cocoa flavanol extract or high-flavanol cocoa powder. Candy bars do not count: the flavanols are destroyed in processing and the sugar works against you.

Caution: many trials were industry-funded; caffeine and theobromine in large amounts.

Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone or ubiquinol)Tier 2
Mild: 100 mgModerate: 200 mgHeavy: 300 mg

Typical drop: 3.4 to 4.8 points on top in pooled trials; a small Cochrane review (50 people) found no effect, and the older 11 to 17 point claims came from uncontrolled studies.

Form: either form, with a fat-containing meal. Often tried with statins; trials for statin muscle aches are mixed.

Caution: may reduce warfarin effect.

Vitamin CTier 2
Mild: 500 mgModerate: 1,000 mg, splitHeavy: 2,000 mg, split

Typical drop: about 3.8 overall, 4.9 in people with high pressure, at about 500 mg a day; works best if you are low.

Form: absorption saturates around 500 mg per dose, so split larger amounts. Buffered forms if your stomach is sensitive.

Caution: high doses raise oxalate kidney stone risk.

Dietary nitrate (beetroot juice, leafy greens)Tier 2
Mild: A large serving of leafy greens dailyModerate: About 400 mg nitrate (about 250 mL beetroot juice)Heavy: 600 to 800 mg nitrate, with your clinician

Typical drop: about 5.3 points in people with high pressure; one meta-analysis was null, and the effect is smaller in older adults.

Form: your mouth bacteria do the conversion: skip antiseptic mouthwash (it raised pressure 2 to 3.5 points in a week).

Caution: beets are high in oxalate (kidney stones); additive with nitrate heart medicines and erectile dysfunction drugs.

Riboflavin (B2), only with MTHFR 677TTTier 3
Mild: 1.6 mg/day (the studied dose)Moderate: 1.6 mg/day within a B complexHeavy: Higher doses: no added pressure benefit shown

Typical drop: about 5.6 points on top, but only in people who carry the MTHFR 677TT genotype (about 10% of many populations). In everyone else, no effect.

Genetics loads the gun. Lifestyle and a personalized protocol decide whether the trigger ever gets pulled. If you have had genetics done, check this variant: it is one of the few where the marker predicts the response.

TaurineTier 3
Mild: 1 gModerate: 1.6 g (the studied dose)Heavy: 3 g

Typical drop: about 3 points in pooled trials; 4.6 over 3.4 net in a 12-week trial of 1.6 g a day in people with high-normal pressure.

Form: powder or capsules; magnesium taurate covers both. Any time of day.

Caution: do not get it from energy drinks.

Vitamin K2 (MK-7)Tier 2
Mild: 100 mcgModerate: 180 mcg (the studied dose)Heavy: 360 mcg

Pipes, not pressure: 180 mcg a day for 3 years reduced arterial stiffness in women past menopause; it activates matrix Gla protein, which keeps calcium out of artery walls. Replication is mixed.

Caution: interferes with warfarin; fine with the newer blood thinners. Pair with vitamin D.

Melatonin, controlled release (night pressure)Tier 2
Mild: 0.5 to 1 mgModerate: 2 to 2.5 mg CRHeavy: 3 to 5 mg CR

Typical drop: about 6 over 3.5 at night only, in small trials (one meta-analysis was manufacturer-authored). On propranolol or atenolol, 2.5 mg nightly improved sleep by about 36 minutes.

Timing: 1 to 2 hours before bed. Caution: morning grogginess; start low.

NattokinaseTier 3
Mild: 2,000 FU (the studied dose)Moderate: 4,000 FU, with your clinicianHeavy: Not recommended higher

Typical drop: about 3.5 over 2.3 in pooled small trials. But the best trial (265 people, 3 years) found zero effect on carotid plaque progression, stiffness or pressure.

Caution: real bleeding risk: avoid with anticoagulants, antiplatelets (including aspirin) and before surgery.

NattokinaseLumbrokinaseSerrapeptase
SourceFermented soyEarthwormSerratia bacteria

PlaqueBest RCT null; positive data open-labelOpen-label Chinese trial positiveNone
BleedingRealRealPoorly studied
GradeTier 3 pressure and plaqueTier 3Tier 3
L-citrulline and L-arginineTier 3
Mild: Citrulline 3 gModerate: Citrulline 6 gHeavy: Not recommended higher

Typical drop: citrulline about 4 over 2.5 in small trials (one major meta-analysis was retracted); arginine about 5.4 over 2.7.

Caution: avoid arginine after a heart attack (more deaths in the VINTAGE MI trial). Both are additive with nitrate heart medicines and erectile dysfunction drugs.

No effect or never tested for pressure: vitamin D (a large pooled analysis was null), tart cherry (21 trials, no effect), vitamin E, PQQ (never tested in people), serrapeptase, IV magnesium for vessel health (a legitimate acute drug, but no evidence periodic infusions improve vessels or long-term pressure), and EDTA chelation (the 2024 TACT2 trial found no benefit). Probiotics: a key pooled analysis was retracted.
◆ BOTANICALS & HOMEOPATHY

Stars: ★★★ multiple randomized trials; ★★☆ some human trials; ★☆☆ mechanism or emerging.

Hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa) tea or extract★★★Tier 2
Mild: 1 cup/dayModerate: 3 cups/day (about 1.25 g dried calyces per cup)Heavy: Standardized extract, with your clinician

Typical drop: about 7 points on top in pooled trials (with very mixed results). Head to head with lisinopril, a standardized hibiscus extract lowered pressure, but less than the drug.

Caution: additive with blood pressure medicines; a small rise in a liver enzyme in some studies; avoid in pregnancy.

Aged garlic extract★★★Tier 2
Mild: 600 mgModerate: 1,200 mg (the studied dose)Heavy: Not recommended above 1,200 mg

Typical drop: about 5 points overall, up to 8.7 in people with high pressure; much of the data comes from one research group using one brand.

Form: aged extract (odorless, stable S-allylcysteine) rather than raw garlic oil. Caution: bleeding with anticoagulants; stop 7 days before surgery.

Olive leaf extract★★☆Tier 2
Mild: 250 mg twice dailyModerate: 500 mg twice daily (the studied dose)Heavy: Not recommended above 500 mg twice daily

Typical drop: about 4 points; one trial matched captopril. Low-certainty evidence.

Caution: additive with pressure and diabetes medicines.

Black seed (Nigella sativa)★★☆Tier 2
Mild: 500 mgModerate: 1 gHeavy: 2 g

Typical drop: about 3.3 over 2.8 in pooled trials of around 8 weeks.

Caution: can lower blood sugar; anticoagulant interactions.

Hawthorn (Crataegus) standardized extract★★☆Tier 2
Mild: 250 mgModerate: 600 mgHeavy: 1,200 mg (the studied dose)

Typical drop: mainly the bottom number, about 3 points; a stronger case for heart failure symptoms than for pressure.

Form: standardized to oligomeric procyanidins. Caution: additive with digoxin, nitrates and pressure medicines.

Ground flaxseed★★☆Tier 2
Mild: 15 g/dayModerate: 30 g/day (the studied dose)Heavy: 45 g/day

Typical drop: about 3 over 2.4 overall; about 10 over 7 in one trial of people with leg artery disease.

Form: freshly ground. Caution: drink fluid; separate from medicines by 2 hours.

Green or black tea★★☆Tier 2
Mild: 2 cupsModerate: 4 cupsHeavy: 5 cups

Typical drop: about 1 to 2 points. Caution: caffeine; concentrated green tea extracts have caused liver injury, so drink it rather than take it.

Celery seed, ginger, cinnamon★☆☆Tier 3

Small or conflicting trials; reasonable as food, not as a treatment. Celery seed is traditionally used as a diuretic (mostly animal data; see Loop diuretics in Medications): avoid in pregnancy; photosensitivity. Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which can harm the liver in large amounts.

Diosmin + hesperidin (micronized purified flavonoid fraction)★★★Tier 2
Mild: 500 mgModerate: 1,000 mg/day (the usual dose)Heavy: 1,000 mg twice daily short-term

For leaky, swollen, heavy legs: leg heaviness down 65% (risk ratio 0.35) and smaller ankles in pooled trials. The old vein remedies have far better evidence than any trendy glycocalyx product.

Caution: stomach upset; much of the data is industry-linked.

Horse chestnut seed extract★★★Tier 2
Mild: Standardized to 50 mg aescin, once dailyModerate: 50 mg aescin twice dailyHeavy: 75 mg aescin twice daily, short-term

For leg swelling: leg volume down about 32 mL vs placebo (Cochrane). Use a standardized extract only; raw seeds are toxic.

Caution: stomach upset; avoid with anticoagulants, in pregnancy, and with kidney or liver disease.

Arterosil HP (rhamnan sulfate from green seaweed)★☆☆Tier 3
Mild: Per labelModerate: Per labelHeavy: Per label

The glycocalyx idea: seaweed rhamnan sulfate supports the vessel's gel coat in mice. Promising in the lab; human trials still to come. Dr. Yoshi likes this one specifically (no financial tie to the company), and it is honestly labeled here as early.

Caution: anticoagulant activity in lab studies: discuss if you take blood thinners. Note: Endocalyx, the best-known glycocalyx supplement, showed no effect in the only independent trial in older adults.

Rauwolfia (Indian snakeroot) is a drug, not a gentle herb. Its active compound is reserpine, a prescription blood pressure medicine that lowered the top number about 8 points in trials but can cause depression, stomach ulcers and nasal congestion. No dose is published here: it belongs only with a prescriber. Real licorice root works the other way and raises pressure.
◆ HOMEOPATHIC OPTIONS TO CONSIDER
Classical homeopathy is highly individualized. Options below are common classical choices for this pattern. A trained homeopath will refine to your specific case. Default working potency 30C; 200C for deeper constitutional work under guidance. This section sits at Tier 3. Homeopathy does not replace blood pressure medication.
Glonoinum, 30C
Prepared from nitroglycerin. Surging, bursting, pounding head with every heartbeat; flushed face; worse from sun and heat; pressure that climbs suddenly. The classical "rush of blood to the head" remedy.
A sudden severe headache with very high pressure (180/120 or higher), confusion, vision change or weakness is an emergency: call emergency services, do not reach for a remedy.
Aurum metallicum, 30C
Gold. The driven, responsible, high-achieving person who carries heavy duty and quiet despair; congestion and high pressure with a sense of failure or grief; worse at night. A constitutional remedy best chosen with a homeopath.
If heaviness ever turns into thoughts of not wanting to live, reach out the same day: call or text 988 in the US, or your clinician.
Natrum muriaticum, 30C
Prepared from salt. Holds grief in and does not cry in front of others; craves salt; worse from sun; hammering headaches. The remedy picture echoes the salt and fluid lever, a nice bridge between the physical and emotional story.
Crataegus mother tincture (Q) · cross-listed as a botanical
Not technically homeopathic: a mother tincture is hawthorn at a material dose, working through ordinary pharmacology, so it carries the same interactions as the hawthorn extract above (digoxin, nitrates, blood pressure medicines). Classical use is about 10 to 20 drops 2 to 3 times a day in water; this tincture regimen itself has not been tested in trials.

Sequencing rule: home numbers first (free, and the most honest), then core labs and a sleep screen, act for 8 to 12 weeks, and escalate to advanced testing only where a real question remains.

Physical capacity

DEXA scan Tier 2

Read far more than body fat: visceral fat (the depot that drives insulin and sodium retention), android vs gynoid distribution, lean and appendicular lean mass, and bone density. Essential on weight-loss injections, where the scale cannot tell fat loss from muscle loss.

Grip strength Tier 2

A validated predictor of mortality, and the same grip you train for isometric pressure work. Track it every few months.

Gait speed Tier 2

A timed 4 to 6 meter walk independently predicts mortality. Slow gait plus dizziness on standing is a reason not to push pressure lower.

Read this first: everything here is an accelerator or an open question, not a substitute for the foundations. Several items are labeled honestly as unproven, because they come up in the Circle and deserve a straight answer.

Devices and procedures

Light & Energy · EECP
Enhanced external counterpulsationTier 2
Leg cuffs squeeze in time with your heartbeat, usually 35 one-hour sessions (offered at specialized centers, for example in Los Angeles). FDA-cleared for angina: in a sham-controlled trial it reduced angina and delayed ischemia. For vessel health, a small sham-controlled trial found lining function (flow-mediated dilation) up 51% vs 2% with sham. One of several therapies to discuss, not a first step. Not suitable with some valve, aortic or clotting conditions.
NATURAL CLOSEST COUSIN
Daily calf-pump work, isometrics and Zone 2 walking push shear stress through the same vessels, at no cost. Smaller per session, but cumulative.
Breath · IMST device
Inspiratory muscle strength trainingTier 2
30 resisted breaths a day at about 75% of your maximum: the top number fell from 135 to 126 in 6 weeks in adults 50 to 79, and lining function improved about 45%. Inexpensive handheld trainers exist; start lower and build up. Small trial; larger trials are under way.
Sound & Frequency · vagus stimulation
Transcutaneous ear (tragus) vagus nerve stimulationTier 3
A gentle ear clip, about 1 hour a day. Promising for the conductor and for POTS (pulse jump 18 vs 32 on sham in 26 women); pressure trials are small and early.
Procedure · renal denervation
Renal denervationTier 2
A catheter procedure that quiets the nerves around the kidney arteries; FDA-approved in late 2023 for uncontrolled high pressure. In sham-controlled trials it lowered pressure about 4 to 6 points more than sham. For people whose pressure stays high despite medication, or who cannot tolerate it. Long-term data still accumulating.

Emerging medicines

Medication · new in 2026
Aldosterone synthase inhibitors and twice-yearly injectionsTier 2
A new class blocks aldosterone production at the source. Baxdrostat (Baxfendy) became the first FDA-approved aldosterone synthase inhibitor in May 2026, for high pressure that is not controlled on other medicines. In its main trial (796 people already taking 2 or more medicines) it lowered the top number about 9 to 10 points more than placebo. Lorundrostat showed similar drops and is under FDA review, with a decision expected by December 2026. Zilebesiran, an RNA-based injection given every 6 months, is in a large outcome trial and is not approved. Strength: they target the fluid lever directly. Shortcomings: no data yet on strokes or heart attacks, and potassium can climb too high (above 6.0 in about 2% to 3% of people on baxdrostat), so potassium and sodium need checking, and potassium salt is off the table while you take one.

Supplements and infusions with more buzz than data

Glycocalyx
Arterosil HP (rhamnan sulfate)Tier 3
Supports the vessel gel coat in mice; human trials still to come. Dr. Yoshi's preferred glycocalyx product (no financial tie to the company), honestly labeled early. Endocalyx, the best-known competitor, showed no effect in the only independent trial in older adults. The most powerful glycocalyx "supplement" may be steady blood sugar: one sugar spike halved it within hours.
Fibrinolytic enzymes
Nattokinase, lumbrokinase, serrapeptaseTier 3
Nattokinase: about 3.5 points off the top in small trials, but no effect on plaque in the best 3-year trial. Lumbrokinase: lowers fibrinogen; low-quality data. Serrapeptase: no vascular action shown. All carry bleeding risk with blood thinners. See the comparison in Nutraceuticals.
Infusions
IV magnesiumTier 3
A legitimate acute drug (seizure prevention in pre-eclampsia, rhythm problems, blunting pressure spikes during surgery), but there is no evidence that periodic IV magnesium improves vessel health or long-term pressure. The only placebo-controlled trial of the Myers cocktail (for fibromyalgia) was negative. Oral magnesium has better, still modest, vascular data.
Chelation
EDTA chelationTier 3
The first TACT trial was intriguing; the 2024 TACT2 trial in people with diabetes and a prior heart attack found no benefit. Not recommended for blood pressure or vessel health.
Water
EZ water, structured water and AnalemmaTier 3
Real lab phenomenon (EZ water), no human pressure data, and a marketing umbrella ("structured water") with no agreed test. Full details and the disclosure are in the Water pillar.
Oxygen
Hyperbaric oxygenTier 3
Raises pressure during sessions. Useful for other indications; get pressure controlled first.
Light
Red light, PEMF and groundingTier 3
A handful of small, biased or uncontrolled studies. Fine to enjoy; not a blood pressure treatment.

Questions that puncture a settled assumption, each with the honest limitation built in. Use them to open a conversation, a call or a video.

Aha Moment 1 · Conventional blind spot
Can a normal blood pressure still shorten your life?
Yes, if you are salt-sensitive. Among people tested with an IV salt load and followed up to 27 years, salt-sensitive people tested after age 25 with normal pressure died at about the same rate as people with high pressure. The caveat: the test was 2 L of IV saline, not food, and the study is observational.
  • Citation: Weinberger MH, Fineberg NS, Fineberg SE, Weinberger M. Hypertension, 2001;37(2 Pt 2):429-432. 708 people, 123 deaths among the 596 traced.
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Opening hook
Aha Moment 2 · Brain and body
Can standing up tell you something about your brain decades from now?
A drop in pressure on standing in middle age tracked with about 54% higher dementia risk over 25 years. The caveat: an association in a large cohort, not proof that the drop causes dementia, but it is a free test you can do today.
  • Citation: Rawlings AM, Juraschek SP, Heiss G, et al. Neurology, 2018;91(8):e759-e768 (ARIC study).
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Before the standing test
Aha Moment 3 · Systems thinking
Is your heart really a pump?
Yes: stop the heart and pressure falls to a few points within seconds. But it has help. In 3-day-old chick embryos with the heart stopped, blood kept moving for about 50 minutes, and infrared light took the flow from 41 to 153 microns a second. The caveat: 6 embryos, microscopic speeds, and infrared also warms tissue. It says the vessel wall and its water may be active players, not that the heart is optional.
  • Citation: Li Z, Pollack GH. PLoS One, 2023;18(10):e0289652.
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: After the 4 pumps
Aha Moment 4 · Timeline and causality
Can one sugary drink strip the lining of your blood vessels?
In healthy young men, raising blood sugar for a few hours halved the glycocalyx, the vessel's protective gel coat (about 1.7 to 0.8 L of glycocalyx volume), and an antioxidant (N-acetylcysteine) blocked it. The caveat: a glucose clamp, not a soda, and a small study. Steady blood sugar may be the most powerful glycocalyx supplement.
  • Citation: Nieuwdorp M, van Haeften TW, Gouverneur MC, et al. Diabetes, 2006;55(2):480-486.
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Pipes section
Aha Moment 5 · Organism and microbiology
Can your mouthwash raise your blood pressure?
Bacteria on your tongue turn the nitrate in greens and beets into nitric oxide. A week of antiseptic mouthwash raised pressure 2 to 3.5 points in healthy volunteers. The caveat: small, short study in healthy people.
  • Citation: Kapil V, Haydar SM, Pearl V, et al. Free Radic Biol Med, 2013;55:93-100.
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Food pillar
Aha Moment 6 · Conventional blind spot
Could cutting salt actually raise your blood pressure?
For roughly 1 in 7 to 1 in 9 people (about 11% to 15% in this group's studies), yes: their pressure rises on a low-salt diet ("inverse salt sensitivity"), as renin, aldosterone and adrenaline climb. The caveat: mainly one research group, and definitions vary. That is why you test instead of guessing.
  • Citation: Felder RA, Gildea JJ, Xu P, et al. Curr Hypertens Rep, 2022;24(9):361-374.
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Before the salt test
Aha Moment 7 · Systems thinking
Can swapping your salt shaker prevent a stroke?
In 20,995 people in rural China, a salt with 25% potassium chloride cut strokes 14% and deaths 12% over 5 years, with no more serious high-potassium events. The caveat: people with kidney disease or potassium-holding drugs were excluded, and baseline salt intake was very high.
  • Citation: Neal B, Wu Y, Feng X, et al. N Engl J Med, 2021;385(12):1067-1077 (SSaSS).
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Choose your salt
Aha Moment 8 · Conventional blind spot
Is doubling your pill the best next step?
Usually not. Adding a second kind of medicine gave about 5 times the extra lowering of doubling the first, across 42 trials and nearly 11,000 people, and lower doses of most classes cause fewer side effects.
  • Citation: Wald DS, Law M, Morris JK, Bestwick JP, Wald NJ. Am J Med, 2009;122(3):290-300. Side effects: Law MR, et al. BMJ, 2003;326:1427.
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Medications
Aha Moment 9 · Timeline and causality
Does it matter whether you take your pill in the morning or at bedtime?
Not for heart attacks or strokes: 2 large trials (21,104 and 3,357 people) found no difference. Take it when you will not forget. The caveat: an earlier trial (Hygia) reported a large benefit and carries an expression of concern.
  • Citation: Mackenzie IS, et al. Lancet, 2022;400:1417-1425 (TIME). Garrison SR, et al. JAMA, 2025;333(23):2061-2072 (BedMed).
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Sleep & Light pillar
Aha Moment 10 · Brain and body
Can 5 minutes of breathing work like a blood pressure pill?
Breathing in hard against a small resistance device, 30 breaths a day, dropped the top number from 135 to 126 in 6 weeks in adults 50 to 79, and most of it was still there 6 weeks after stopping. The caveat: 36 people; larger trials are under way.
  • Citation: Craighead DH, Heinbockel TC, Freeberg KA, et al. J Am Heart Assoc, 2021;10(13):e020980.
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Air pillar
Aha Moment 11 · Brain and body
Can loneliness raise your blood pressure?
In adults 50 to 68, loneliness predicted the top number climbing faster year after year, independent of age, health conditions, medications, stress and depression, with the loneliest rising an estimated 14.4 points more over 4 years than the least lonely (a model projection). The caveat: 229 people, observational.
  • Citation: Hawkley LC, Thisted RA, Masi CM, Cacioppo JT. Psychol Aging, 2010;25(1):132-141.
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Community pillar or closing
Aha Moment 12 · Conventional blind spot
Can your bottom number be too low?
In 22,672 people with blocked heart arteries, a bottom number under 60 went with about twice the heart events of 70 to 79. The heart muscle feeds itself between beats. The caveat: observational; a low bottom number partly marks stiffer, sicker arteries. Lower is still better for most people who tolerate it.
  • Citation: Vidal-Petiot E, Ford I, Greenlaw N, et al. Lancet, 2016;388(10056):2142-2152 (CLARIFY).
  • Delivery tip: Drop it, pause 3 to 5 seconds, then answer.
  • Best placed: Is lower always better?
